chapters.title: Preaching and Teaching in Jewish Practice
chapters.subtitle: How the synagogue taught Scripture, and how Jesus taught within that world
chapters.nutshell: In Jesus' day, Scripture was read aloud in the synagogue, translated, and then explained in a sermon. Teachers sat to teach, students sat at their feet, and learning meant memorising, repeating and asking questions. Jesus taught inside this world, yet people noticed that he taught "with authority".
chapters.bigIdea: Jesus' preaching and teaching make the most sense against the background of synagogue reading, sermon and study.
skeleton: The synagogue service: prayer, reading, translation, sermon
The teacher sits; the disciple sits at his feet
Sermon forms: proem, legal question, hopeful ending, parable
Study by memory, repetition, questions and partners

p: On the Sabbath the community gathered to pray and to hear Scripture. The service included the Shema, the prayer later called the Amidah, a reading from the Torah, a reading from the Prophets (the Haftarah) and often a sermon. Many details of the first-century order are known only from later Jewish sources, so the exact shape is debated, but the main parts are clear.

Because many people spoke Aramaic rather than Hebrew, a translator (the meturgeman) put the Torah into Aramaic one verse at a time, and the Prophets up to three verses at a time (Mishnah Megillah 4:4).

In Nazareth Jesus stood up to read from Isaiah, gave the scroll back to the attendant and sat down; then he began to teach (Luke 4:16–21). Sitting was the posture of a teacher (Matt 5:1; 23:2). In Pisidian Antioch the synagogue rulers invited Paul to give "a word of exhortation" after the readings (Acts 13:15) — a common name for a sermon (compare Heb 13:22).

Later rabbinic collections show set sermon forms. The petichta (proem) opened with a distant verse, often from the Writings, and wound its way to the day's reading. The yelammedenu sermon began with a legal question ("Let our teacher instruct us…"). Sermons often ended with a word of hope (chatimah). These forms are known from collections written down centuries after Jesus, so we cannot be sure how far they were used in his day.
Teachers loved the mashal (parable) followed by the nimshal (its application): "To what may this be compared?" Jesus' parables belong to this family.

A disciple (talmid) sat "at the feet" of a teacher (Luke 10:39; Acts 22:3; Mishnah Avot 1:4). Children learned to read Scripture in the beit sefer (house of the book); older students studied in the beit midrash (house of study). Learning was by memory, repetition and chanting aloud, with many questions. Later tradition prizes the chavruta, a study partner who argues the text with you.
Jesus gave his disciples authority to "bind and loose" (Matt 16:19; 18:18). Many scholars connect this with rabbinic usage, where "binding" and "loosing" meant forbidding and permitting.

Jesus used the methods of his people — parables, questions, "how much more" arguments and Scripture quotations. What amazed his hearers was not a new method but his authority: he taught "as one who had authority, and not as the scribes" (Mark 1:22). Scribes usually supported a ruling by citing earlier teachers; Jesus said, "But I say to you" (Matt 5:22).

diagrams.title: A synagogue service in Jesus' day (simplified)
diagrams.note: The order is reconstructed partly from later sources; local practice varied.

steps.d: "Hear, O Israel…" (Deut 6:4–9) with blessings before and after.
Standing prayer of blessings; its fixed wording developed over time.
Several readers in turn; the scroll handed out by the attendant (Luke 4:17, 20).
Aramaic rendering, verse by verse for the Torah (Mishnah Megillah 4:4).
A matching reading from the Prophets — as Jesus read Isaiah 61 (Luke 4:17–19).
A "word of exhortation" explaining the readings (Acts 13:15).
The service closed with a priestly blessing when a priest was present (Num 6:24–26).

diagrams.title: Who is who in synagogue and study

cells: cares for scrolls, hands them out
expert in writing and the Law

cards.front: "What man of you, having a hundred sheep…?"
cards.back: A short story from daily life, followed by its point (nimshal). Rabbis used the same pattern: a king, a son, a field. Jesus' parables draw hearers in, then turn the story on them.
cards.echo: Rabbinic parables often begin "To what may this be compared?"

cards.front: "Who do you say that I am?"
cards.back: Jesus asked questions and often answered a question with a question. This made people think for themselves, a hallmark of Jewish study.
cards.echo: Study in the beit midrash moved by question and answer.

cards.front: "If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts…"
cards.back: The light-and-heavy argument (kal va-chomer): if something is true in a small case, it is even more true in a great case.
cards.echo: The first of Hillel's rules of interpretation.

cards.front: A camel through the eye of a needle
cards.back: Startling pictures fix a truth in the memory: a log in your own eye, a camel through a needle. Hearers knew this was picture language, not literal instruction.
cards.echo: Teachers used memorable sayings so students would never forget.

cards.front: He took a child and set him among them
cards.back: Jesus taught by doing: placing a child in the middle, washing feet, cursing a fig tree. Like the prophets' signs, the action carried the message.
Jesus answered opponents by quoting and reasoning from the Torah, Prophets and Psalms, sometimes from a single word or tense of a verse.
cards.echo: The same close reading is found in midrash.

places.d: His home synagogue: he read Isaiah and preached that it was fulfilled.
He taught in the synagogue on the Sabbath and people were amazed at his authority.
A first-century synagogue has been excavated here, showing what Galilean synagogues looked like.
As a boy he sat among the teachers in the Temple, listening and asking questions; later he taught daily in its courts.

verses.text: He rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant and sat down… "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing."
He taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.
After the reading of the Law and the Prophets… "If you have any word of exhortation for the people, say it."
Brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel.

keyPoints: The synagogue service centred on prayer, reading Scripture, translating it and explaining it.
A teacher sat to teach; disciples sat at his feet and learned by memory, repetition and questions.
Rabbinic sermon forms (petichta, yelammedenu, hopeful ending) are known from later collections.
Jesus' parables, questions and "how much more" arguments are Jewish teaching methods.
What stood out was his authority: "But I say to you."
reflect: Which of Jesus' teaching methods helps you remember his words best, and why?
How could memorising, repeating and asking questions change the way you study Scripture?

quiz.q: What did the meturgeman do in the synagogue?
quiz.why: He rendered the Hebrew reading into Aramaic, verse by verse for the Torah (Mishnah Megillah 4:4).

quiz.q: What posture did a teacher take when teaching?
quiz.why: Jesus sat down to teach (Luke 4:20; Matt 5:1); teachers sat on "Moses' seat" (Matt 23:2).
It opens "Let our teacher instruct us…" with a question of law, then moves to the reading.

quiz.q: What amazed people about Jesus' teaching in Mark 1:22?
options: He taught with authority, not as the scribes
quiz.why: He did not only quote earlier teachers; he spoke with his own authority.

terms.def: The translator who rendered the Hebrew readings into Aramaic in the synagogue.
A sermon "opening" that starts from a distant verse and leads to the day's reading.
"House of study", where older students studied Scripture and tradition.
A study partner; learning in pairs by discussion and debate.
Rabbinic terms for forbidding and permitting; used by Jesus in Matt 16:19 and 18:18.

chapters.title: From Birth to Death: Jewish Life Customs
chapters.subtitle: The customs behind the births, weddings and funerals of the Gospels
chapters.nutshell: A Jewish life in Jesus' day was marked by customs from the Torah and from tradition: circumcision and naming on the eighth day, purification and the Temple offering, schooling, betrothal and wedding, and careful burial and mourning. Knowing them makes many Gospel scenes come alive.
chapters.bigIdea: From the eighth day to the ossuary, Jewish life customs explain much of what happens in the Gospels.
skeleton: Sickness, old age, death and mourning

p: A baby boy was circumcised on the eighth day (Gen 17:12; Lev 12:3), the sign of God's covenant with Abraham. The child was named at that time, as with John the Baptist and Jesus (Luke 1:59–63; 2:21).

After childbirth a mother waited 40 days for a son or 80 for a daughter, then brought an offering to the Temple: a lamb and a bird, or, if poor, two doves or two young pigeons (Lev 12). Mary and Joseph brought the poor family's offering (Luke 2:22–24). A firstborn son was redeemed for five shekels (Num 18:15–16).

Weaning could come at two or three years and was celebrated with a feast (Gen 21:8; compare 2 Macc 7:27). A later saying gives the stages of learning: Scripture at five, Mishnah at ten, the commandments at thirteen, marriage at eighteen (Mishnah Avot 5:21). Jesus went up to Jerusalem at twelve (Luke 2:42). The bar mitzvah ceremony itself is a later, medieval development.
Boys normally learned their father's trade; Jesus was known as the carpenter's son (Matt 13:55).

Marriage had two stages. Betrothal (kiddushin or erusin) made the couple legally bound; ending it needed a divorce (Matt 1:18–19). A contract (ketubah) set out the husband's duties. Some months later the bridegroom brought the bride to his home under the canopy or bridal chamber (chuppah) — the wedding proper (nissuin) — followed by up to seven days of feasting (Judg 14:12).
The friend of the bridegroom helped arrange things and rejoiced at the groom's voice (John 3:29).

Life centred on the home and the Sabbath meal. Visiting the sick was a deed of love; James tells elders to pray and anoint the sick with oil (Jas 5:14). The old were honoured: "You shall rise up before the grey head" (Lev 19:32).

Burial was quick, usually the same day (compare Deut 21:23; Acts 5:6). The body was washed (Acts 9:37), wrapped in linen with spices (John 19:39–40) and laid in a family tomb cut in rock, often closed with a stone. About a year later the bones were gathered into a stone box (ossuary). Some scholars link "let the dead bury their own dead" (Matt 8:22) to this second burial.

Mourners tore their clothes, sat for seven days of mourning (shiva; Gen 50:10) while friends came to comfort them (John 11:19), and observed a lighter thirty-day period. Families hired mourning women and flute players (Jer 9:17; Matt 9:23).

diagrams.title: A Jewish life from day one to the ossuary

events.d: Midwives helped; the baby was washed, rubbed with salt and wrapped in cloths (Ezek 16:4; Luke 2:7).
Offering at the Temple; two birds if poor (Lev 12; Luke 2:22–24).
Scripture at 5, Mishnah at 10 (Mishnah Avot 5:21 — a later saying).
Jesus in the Temple at 12 (Luke 2:42); "commandments at 13". Bar mitzvah ceremony is medieval.
Washed, wrapped in linen with spices, laid in a tomb (Acts 9:37; John 19:40).
Bones gathered into an ossuary in the family tomb.

nodes.d: Families agree; a bride-price (mohar) is settled (Gen 34:12).
Legally binding; a ketubah lists the husband's duties (Matt 1:18).
Often about a year; the groom prepares a home (compare John 14:2–3).
Night procession with lamps to fetch the bride (Matt 25:1–13).
The bride enters the groom's home and bridal chamber; the marriage is complete.
Celebration with guests and the friend of the bridegroom (Judg 14:12; John 2:1–10; 3:29).

steps.d: Eyes closed; relatives tear their clothes (Gen 37:34; 2 Sam 1:11).
Washed (Acts 9:37), anointed, wrapped in linen with spices (John 19:39–40).
Same-day burial; flute players and wailing women (Jer 9:17; Matt 9:23; Luke 7:12).
Laid on a shelf in a family tomb; a stone rolled across the door (Mark 15:46).
Mourners stay home; friends come to comfort (Gen 50:10; John 11:19).
A lighter period of mourning (compare Deut 34:8).
About a year later the bones are gathered into a stone box.

diagrams.title: Six Gospel scenes explained by life customs

cards.back: The name was given at the circumcision on the eighth day, and a boy was usually named after a relative. "None of your relatives is called by this name," they said — so Zechariah's written answer amazed them.
cards.echo: Circumcision on the eighth day, Gen 17:12.

cards.front: What does Mary's offering tell us?
cards.back: The Torah allowed a family who could not afford a lamb to bring two birds. Mary and Joseph brought the poor family's offering: the Son of God was born into a poor home.
cards.echo: "Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor" (2 Cor 8:9).

cards.front: Why is Jesus' age, twelve, mentioned?
cards.back: A boy was nearing the age when he would take on the commandments. Jesus sits among the teachers, listening and asking questions — the way of a good student.
Wedding feasts could last days, and the host's family had to provide. Running out of wine brought public shame. Jesus quietly saves the family's honour with the best wine.
cards.echo: The messianic banquet with abundant wine (Isa 25:6).

cards.back: Even poor families hired flute players and mourning women. When Jesus said the girl was sleeping, the hired mourners laughed at him.

cards.front: Why did so many people come to Martha and Mary?
cards.back: Friends came to comfort the family during the seven days of mourning. Lazarus had been buried the same day and was four days in the tomb — beyond any doubt dead.

verses.text: At the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus.
…to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, "a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons."
The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice.
They took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
You shall stand up before the grey head and honour the face of an old man.

keyPoints: Boys were circumcised and named on the eighth day.
Mary and Joseph brought the poor family's offering of two birds.
Marriage had two stages: a binding betrothal, then the wedding and feast.
Burial was quick, with washing, linen and spices; bones were later placed in an ossuary.
Seven days of mourning (shiva) and hired mourners appear in the Gospel stories.
reflect: Which Gospel scene looks different to you now that you know the custom behind it?
What does Jesus' birth into a poor family, with its simple offering, say to you?

quiz.q: On which day was a Jewish boy circumcised and named?
What did Mary and Joseph's offering of birds show?
quiz.why: Two birds were allowed for those who could not afford a lamb (Lev 12:8; Luke 2:24).

quiz.q: Why did Joseph plan to divorce Mary though they were not yet living together?
quiz.why: Betrothal (kiddushin/erusin) was a binding stage of marriage (Matt 1:18–19).

options: A stone box for the bones in second burial
quiz.why: About a year after death the bones were gathered into an ossuary.

terms.def: Circumcision, the covenant sign, on the eighth day.
Betrothal, the first and legally binding stage of marriage.
The marriage contract listing the husband's duties.
The canopy or bridal chamber; the wedding proper (nissuin).
The seven days of mourning after a burial.
A stone box into which bones were gathered about a year after death.
